SEARCH
Package neqsim.mathlib.linearalgebra

Interface LinearAlgebraOperations

All Known Implementing Classes:
EjmlLinearAlgebra, JamaLinearAlgebra
public interface LinearAlgebraOperations
Dense linear-algebra operations, independent of the library that performs them.

NeqSim depends on four linear-algebra libraries (JAMA, EJML, Apache Commons Math and MTJ) and repeats the same dense Gaussian elimination in many private helper methods. This interface is the single contract those implementations are held to, so a caller can select a backend without changing any calling code.

Matrices are rectangular, row-major double[][] values, where matrix[row][column] is the entry at that position and every row has the same length. Vectors are double[] values. Each operation documents its dimension requirements; in particular, direct solves, inversion and determinants require square matrices, while least-squares solves require at least as many rows as columns and full column rank. No library type appears in a signature.

Implementations must not modify their arguments, must return newly allocated arrays, and must be stateless and safe for concurrent use. Invalid dimensions, non-finite inputs and detected solver failures are reported as a LinearAlgebraException, rather than through backend-specific failure signals. A finite solve or inverse result is not an accuracy guarantee: least squares checks numerical rank, but direct LU solves and inversion do not apply a rank or conditioning threshold.

Validation and defensive array conversions add work and allocations. This interface makes no speedup guarantee; benchmark complete representative solver workloads before migrating performance-critical loops or choosing a backend.

Structured systems are deliberately out of scope. Use TDMAsolve for tridiagonal systems and BandedLinearSystemSolver for banded systems, both of which exploit a storage format that a dense interface would discard.

  • Method Details

    • getName

      String getName()
      Name of the backend performing the operations, for logging and benchmark reporting.
      Returns:
      a short backend name such as EJML

    • solve

      double[] solve(double[][] matrixA, double[] vectorB)
      Solve the square system A x = b.

      Uses LU without a numerical rank or conditioning threshold. An ill-conditioned matrix can yield a finite but inaccurate result, even when rank(double[][]) reports numerical rank deficiency. Use conditionNumber(double[][]) and residual checks to assess suitability for the caller's accuracy target.

      Parameters:
      matrixA - square coefficient matrix
      vectorB - right-hand-side vector with one entry per row of matrixA
      Returns:
      the solution vector
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the matrix is not square, the dimensions disagree, any entry is non-finite, or the backend reports a failed factorisation or the computed solution contains a non-finite entry

    • solveLeastSquares

      double[] solveLeastSquares(double[][] matrixA, double[] vectorB)
      Solve A x = b in the least-squares sense, minimising the Euclidean norm of the residual.

      Use this for over-determined systems from parameter fitting with full column rank. Rank-deficient systems are rejected; this method is not a pseudoinverse fallback. For a well-conditioned square system it returns the same answer as solve(double[][], double[]) but generally costs more.

      Parameters:
      matrixA - coefficient matrix with at least as many rows as columns
      vectorB - right-hand-side vector with one entry per row of matrixA
      Returns:
      the least-squares solution, one entry per column of matrixA
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the dimensions disagree, any entry is non-finite, or the matrix does not have full column rank

    • invert

      double[][] invert(double[][] matrix)
      Compute the inverse of a square matrix.

      Prefer solve(double[][], double[]) when the inverse is only needed to multiply a right-hand side; an explicit inverse is both slower and numerically weaker. Use this only when the inverse itself is the result, as in a covariance or sensitivity matrix. As with solve(double[][], double[]), no numerical rank or conditioning threshold is applied; a finite inverse can still be inaccurate for an ill-conditioned matrix.

      Parameters:
      matrix - square matrix to invert
      Returns:
      the inverse matrix
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the matrix is not square, any entry is non-finite, the backend reports a failed factorisation or the computed inverse contains a non-finite entry

    • subtract

      double[] subtract(double[] vectorA, double[] vectorB)
      Subtract one vector from another of the same length.

      With scale(double[], double) this expresses the damped Newton update x = x - damping * dx on the vectors returned by solve(double[][], double[]).

      Parameters:
      vectorA - vector to subtract from
      vectorB - vector to subtract, with the same length as vectorA
      Returns:
      the difference vectorA - vectorB
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the lengths disagree or any entry is non-finite

    • scale

      double[] scale(double[] vector, double factor)
      Multiply every entry of a vector by a scalar.

      Throws:

    • rank

      int rank(double[][] matrix)
      Determine the numerical rank of a matrix.

      The rank is the number of singular values above a tolerance scaled by the largest singular value and the matrix dimensions, so a matrix that is singular only to within rounding error is reported as rank deficient.

      Parameters:
      matrix - matrix of any shape
      Returns:
      the numerical rank, between zero and the smaller of the two dimensions
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the rows have unequal length or any entry is non-finite

    • conditionNumber

      double conditionNumber(double[][] matrix)
      Compute the two-norm condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value.

      A value near one indicates a well-conditioned matrix. A value comparable with the reciprocal of machine epsilon, about 1.0e16 in double precision, means a solution carries no significant digits.

      Parameters:
      matrix - matrix of any shape
      Returns:
      the condition number, or Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY if the matrix is numerically rank deficient, using the same tolerance as rank(double[][])
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the rows have unequal length or any entry is non-finite

    • determinant

      double determinant(double[][] matrix)
      Compute the determinant of a square matrix.

      A determinant is a poor test for singularity because it scales with the size of the entries; prefer conditionNumber(double[][]) or rank(double[][]) for that. Use this where the determinant itself is the quantity of interest.

      Parameters:
      matrix - square matrix
      Returns:
      the determinant
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the matrix is not square or any entry is non-finite

    • euclideanNorm

      double euclideanNorm(double[] vector)
      Compute the Euclidean length of a vector, the square root of the sum of the squared entries.

      This is the norm wanted by an iterative solver testing a residual or a step for convergence.

      Parameters:
      vector - vector to measure
      Returns:
      the Euclidean norm
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the vector is empty or any entry is non-finite

    • spectralNorm

      double spectralNorm(double[][] matrix)
      Compute the induced two-norm of a matrix, which is its largest singular value.

      This requires a singular value decomposition and so costs far more than oneNorm(double[][]). For a single-column matrix it equals the Euclidean length, but euclideanNorm(double[]) computes that directly and should be preferred inside an iteration.

      Parameters:
      matrix - matrix to measure
      Returns:
      the spectral norm
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the rows have unequal length or any entry is non-finite

    • submatrix

      double[][] submatrix(double[][] matrix, int firstRow, int lastRow, int firstColumn, int lastColumn)
      Extract a rectangular block of a matrix.

      Both bounds are inclusive, so submatrix(m, 0, 1, 0, 1) returns the leading two by two block.

      Parameters:
      matrix - matrix to read from
      firstRow - index of the first row to include
      lastRow - index of the last row to include
      firstColumn - index of the first column to include
      lastColumn - index of the last column to include
      Returns:
      the extracted block
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if the matrix is invalid or any bound lies outside it or is out of order

    • withSubmatrix

      double[][] withSubmatrix(double[][] matrix, int firstRow, int firstColumn, double[][] block)
      Copy a matrix with a rectangular block overwritten.

      The argument is left untouched, unlike the in-place block assignment the backends offer. The extent written is given by the dimensions of block, whose top-left corner lands on firstRow, firstColumn.

      Parameters:
      matrix - matrix to copy
      firstRow - row index where the block starts
      firstColumn - column index where the block starts
      block - values to write
      Returns:
      a new matrix carrying the block
      Throws:
      LinearAlgebraException - if either matrix is invalid or the block does not fit at the given corner
